title: Gaseous Exchange
seo_title: Grade 11 Life Sciences: Gaseous Exchange Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_text: The need for gaseous exchange; the structure of the human respiratory system; breathing (inhalation and exhalation); gaseous exchange in the alveoli; transport of gases in the blood; homeostatic control of breathing; diseases of the respiratory system. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 11, Life Sciences: Gaseous exchange)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): the respiratory system, breathing, gaseous exchange in the alveoli, transport of gases and respiratory diseases. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Gases diffuse across the thin walls of the alveoli.
key_sub: The diaphragm contracts and flattens when you breathe in.
body_html:
How to think about it

Air passes through the nose, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli. When you inhale, the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the intercostal muscles lift the ribs; the volume of the chest increases, the pressure falls and air flows in.

Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, where it binds to haemoglobin; carbon dioxide diffuses out. Alveoli have a large surface area, thin moist walls and a good blood supply. A rise in blood CO₂ is detected by the medulla oblongata, which increases the breathing rate. Smoking causes emphysema and lung cancer; tuberculosis is a bacterial lung disease.

Example

What happens to the diaphragm when you breathe out?

It relaxes.

Answer: it relaxes and becomes dome-shaped

Example

Which gas level controls the breathing rate?

Detected by the medulla

Answer: carbon dioxide

Common mistakes

  • Thinking air pushes the lungs open.
  • Thinking oxygen levels mainly control breathing.
  • Mixing up the trachea and the oesophagus.

faq.q: How does smoking harm the lungs?
faq.a: Tar damages the cilia and alveoli, causing emphysema, bronchitis and lung cancer.

faq.q: Why are alveoli surrounded by capillaries?
faq.a: So that gases have only a short distance to diffuse, and blood keeps the concentration gradient high.

items.q: During inspiration (breathing in), what happens to the diaphragm?
items.e: Breathing in: external intercostals and diaphragm contract, ribs up and out, thorax volume up, pressure down, air rushes in. Breathing out is the reverse.

items.q: A person breathes 14 times a minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. How much air does he breathe in each minute?
items.e: Pulmonary ventilation = rate × TV = 14 × 500 = 7 000 mL.

items.q: Which structure stops food from entering the windpipe?
items.e: It is a flap of cartilage.

items.q: What is emphysema?
